buildUp: You need a turning force from stored electricity, and the most power-dense way is a motor whose rotor carries permanent magnets, so it needs no current of its own and runs cooler and more efficiently.

Permanent magnets need a rotating field to follow, so the stator gets three-phase windings, and the battery's DC must be turned into three-phase AC by an inverter built from fast silicon-carbide switches.
To place that field exactly where it should be relative to the magnets, the controller has to know the rotor's angle at every instant, so a resolver sits on the shaft to measure it.
A small motor makes a lot of power only by spinning fast, up to about 18,000 rpm, so a two-stage gearbox steps that down about nine to one to suit the wheels.
On a corner the outer wheel travels further than the inner, so a differential splits the drive between them and lets them turn at different speeds.
Losses of even a few percent of hundreds of kilowatts are several kilowatts of heat, so oil is pumped over the windings and coolant through the inverter's floor, and both end up in a heat exchanger.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Use a magnetic field that rotates, and let a rotor full of permanent magnets chase it round. Fast electronic switches chop the battery's direct current into three carefully timed alternating currents, which set the field spinning at exactly the speed and strength the driver asks for. A simple fixed gear then trades the motor's high speed for the strong, slow twist the wheels need.

hardParts.title: Switching hundreds of amps in a fraction of a microsecond
hardParts.why: The power modules must turn up to roughly 1,000 A on and off tens of thousands of times a second at around 400 V, and every switch wastes a little energy as heat. That's because each time a transistor switches, there's a brief moment when it carries current and has voltage across it. Silicon carbide makes this possible because it switches faster and tolerates more heat than ordinary silicon.

hardParts.title: A rotor that must not fly apart
hardParts.why: At 18,000 rpm the rotor's surface moves at about 500 km/h, and the magnets buried in it are flung outwards with enormous force. The steel holding them in has to be strong, yet any extra steel near the magnets leaks magnetic field and weakens the motor, so the slots are shaped to a fraction of a millimetre to balance strength against performance. Hot magnets also lose strength, so they must be kept cool too.

hardParts.title: Packing in copper and getting the heat out
hardParts.why: More copper in the stator means less resistance and less heat, so the windings are flat hairpin bars that fill about 70 percent of each slot instead of about 45 percent with round wire. Each hairpin has to be bent, inserted and laser welded at its end, a few hundred welds per stator, and oil is sprayed onto the end turns to carry heat away.

principles.explanation: Opposite magnetic poles attract, so if you could move a north pole around a circle, a magnet on a spindle would follow it. The stator does this without moving parts: three sets of copper windings, each fed a current that peaks a third of a cycle after the one before, add up to a single magnetic field that sweeps round smoothly. The rotor's magnets are pulled along just behind the field, and the further behind they lag, the harder they're pulled. Speed up the currents' rhythm and the rotor speeds up; make them stronger and it pushes harder.
principles.title: Magnets chasing a moving field

principles.explanation: Switching the battery voltage on and off very fast, and varying how long each pulse lasts, makes an average that traces out a smooth alternating wave with almost no waste. Flick a light on and off fast enough and it just looks dimmer: what you see is the average. The inverter's transistors do it about 10,000 to 20,000 times a second. The motor's windings smooth the current further, because current in a coil can't change instantly. A switch that is fully on or fully off barely heats up, which leaves the inverter roughly 98 to 99 percent efficient.
principles.title: Making AC by flicking a switch very fast

principles.explanation: Gears can't change a shaft's power, only swap twist for speed, so a small motor spinning fast can be geared down to give the wheels a huge twist. The power a shaft carries is how hard it twists multiplied by how fast it turns. A motor making about 400 N m at 6,000 rpm is delivering roughly 250 kW. Step the speed down about nine times and the twist goes up about nine times, which is how a motor no bigger than a beer keg can push a two-tonne car hard from a standstill.
principles.title: Power is torque times speed

principles.explanation: The iron core is built from thin, insulated sheets because a solid block would carry swirling eddy currents that waste energy as heat. The stator and rotor are made of iron because it channels magnetic field hundreds of times better than air. But a changing field drives swirling currents in any solid conductor, called eddy currents, and these just make heat. Building the core from a stack of sheets only about 0.3 mm thick, each insulated from the next, breaks those swirls up into tiny loops, cutting the loss dramatically.
principles.title: Why the steel is sliced thin

firstPrinciples.problem: Turn the electricity stored in a battery into the force that turns a car's wheels, from a standing start to motorway speed, while wasting as little energy as possible. The battery gives a steady, one-way voltage, but a motor needs a constantly changing current, and the wheels want huge twisting force at low speed while an efficient motor wants to spin fast. All of it has to be small, quiet, cool and last the life of the car.

questions.answer: A petrol engine makes useful power only in a narrow band of speeds and none at standstill, so it needs gears to stay in that band. An electric motor makes strong torque from zero rpm and works well up to about 18,000 rpm, so one fixed ratio covers everything.
questions.question: Why doesn't an electric car need a gearbox with several gears like a petrol car?

questions.answer: The spinning magnets now sweep their field past the windings, which generates current just like a dynamo. The inverter times its switching so that current flows back into the battery, and the effort of making it slows the car.
questions.question: When you lift off the accelerator, how does the same motor recharge the battery?

questions.answer: A changing magnetic field drives wasteful swirling currents in solid metal. Insulated thin sheets break those currents into tiny loops, so far less energy is turned into heat.
questions.question: Why is the motor's iron built from a stack of thin sheets rather than a solid block?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: The whole unit is roughly 90 percent efficient from battery to wheels, against about 30 percent for a petrol engine, and it gets there with a single gear, no clutch and almost nothing that rubs. The real advance is in software and switches: by measuring the rotor angle and adjusting the currents tens of thousands of times a second, the inverter gives the driver instant, smooth torque and turns the motor into a generator whenever they slow down.

name: Electric Car Drive Unit
overview:
A drive unit is what an electric car has where a petrol car has its engine and gearbox. It sits between the rear wheels and turns electricity from the battery into the torque that turns them.

It has three main parts. The inverter on top takes the battery's direct current and, by switching transistors thousands of times a second, turns it into three-phase alternating current. That current flows through copper windings in the motor's stator and makes a rotating magnetic field. The rotor, studded with permanent magnets, is dragged round by that field, up to about 18,000 rpm, with no contact and almost no wear.

That speed is far too high for the wheels, so a two-stage gearbox steps it down about nine to one. The differential then lets the left and right wheels turn at different speeds through corners. There's no clutch and no gear changing: one ratio covers everything from a standing start to top speed, and when you lift off, the motor works as a generator to recharge the battery.

parts.description: Cast-aluminium cover sealing the inverter electronics against water and dust.

details.didYouKnow: Inverter lids often carry a warning label because opening one can expose parts still charged by the capacitor; technicians wait for it to discharge before touching anything inside.
details.howItWorks: The lid bolts down onto the inverter housing over a rubber or formed-in-place gasket, so the delicate electronics stay dry even when the car drives through deep puddles or gets pressure-washed. Being metal, it also acts as part of a shielded box that keeps the fast-switching electrical noise inside from interfering with the car's radio and other electronics.
keyNumbers: Sealing typically meets IP67: dust-tight and survives immersion to about 1 m
Wall thickness roughly 2 to 4 mm
Usually held by around 10 to 20 small bolts
details.madeOf: Usually die-cast or pressed aluminium, which is light, easy to shape with stiffening ribs, and conducts well enough to work as an electromagnetic shield.

parts.name: Inverter lid

parts.description: Microcontroller and gate drivers that switch the transistors thousands of times a second to shape the motor current.

details.didYouKnow: Most of the clever behaviour of an electric motor, such as smooth launches and regenerative braking, lives in this board's software, which is why some cars gain power or efficiency through over-the-air updates.
details.howItWorks: A microcontroller reads the driver's accelerator request, the rotor angle from the resolver and current sensors on each phase, then calculates thousands of times a second exactly when each transistor should switch. Isolated gate-driver chips turn those low-voltage logic signals into the stronger pulses that flip the power modules on and off, while keeping the hundreds of volts on the power side safely separated from the logic side.
keyNumbers: Switching commands typically issued at about 10 to 20 kHz
Control loop runs roughly every 50 to 100 microseconds
Logic side runs at about 3.3 to 5 V, isolated from about 350 to 400 V
details.madeOf: A multilayer glass-fibre circuit board (FR-4) with soldered chips, often given a thin conformal coating to protect against moisture and vibration.

parts.name: Control board

parts.description: Silicon-carbide MOSFETs that turn the battery's DC into one of the three AC phases driving the motor.

details.didYouKnow: The Model 3 was widely reported as the first mass-market car to use silicon-carbide transistors in its main inverter, a move much of the industry later followed.
details.howItWorks: Each phase has a high-side and a low-side switch; turning them on and off in turn connects the U output alternately to the battery's plus and minus. By varying how long each switch stays on (pulse-width modulation), the inverter makes the average voltage rise and fall like a sine wave, and the motor's windings smooth those pulses into a near-sinusoidal current.
keyNumbers: Handles peak currents of very roughly 500 to 1,000 A
SiC chips can run at up to about 175 °C
Switch transitions take well under a microsecond
details.madeOf: Silicon-carbide chips soldered or sintered onto a copper-and-ceramic substrate, encased in plastic, with a copper base that presses onto the coolant-cooled floor of the housing.

parts.name: Power module, phase U

parts.description: Silicon-carbide MOSFETs that turn the battery's DC into one of the three AC phases driving the motor.

details.didYouKnow: Silicon carbide is so hard that it was first used as an abrasive called carborundum, long before anyone made transistors from it.
details.howItWorks: Phase V does the same job as U but runs 120 degrees later in the electrical cycle, so the three phases together create a magnetic field that rotates smoothly around the stator. The control board staggers its switching pattern, and the module sends its output down busbar V into the motor windings.
keyNumbers: Phases spaced 120 degrees apart electrically
Inverter efficiency typically about 98 to 99 percent
Blocking voltage rating typically about 650 V for a 400 V car
details.madeOf: Silicon carbide, a hard compound of silicon and carbon, is used instead of ordinary silicon because it blocks high voltage in a thinner layer and wastes less energy each time it switches.

parts.name: Power module, phase V

parts.description: Silicon-carbide MOSFETs that turn the battery's DC into one of the three AC phases driving the motor.

details.didYouKnow: Because SiC switches waste so little energy, a SiC inverter can add a few percent to a car's range compared with an older silicon-IGBT inverter, with the same battery.
details.howItWorks: The W module completes the set: at any instant the currents in U, V and W add up to zero, so current flowing out through one phase returns through the others. During regenerative braking the same switches run in reverse, rectifying the motor's generated AC back into DC to charge the battery.
keyNumbers: Losses per module typically only tens to a few hundred watts
Each SiC die is only a few millimetres across
Coolant beneath it is usually kept below about 65 °C
details.madeOf: Plastic-moulded package around SiC dies; the chips are bonded to the leads with aluminium or copper wires or ribbons, and the module is mounted with thermal paste or sintered silver to pass heat into the coolant plate.

parts.name: Power module, phase W

parts.description: Film capacitor that smooths the battery current feeding the power modules.

details.didYouKnow: Metallised film capacitors are self-healing: if a tiny spark punches through the film, the thin metal around the hole vaporises and isolates the fault, and the capacitor keeps working.
details.howItWorks: When the transistors switch, they demand sudden bursts of current far faster than the battery cable can deliver because of its inductance. The capacitor sits right beside the power modules and supplies those bursts locally, keeping the DC voltage steady and stopping ripple and voltage spikes from travelling back to the battery.
keyNumbers: Capacitance typically several hundred microfarads
Rated at roughly 450 to 500 V DC
Film only a few micrometres thick
details.madeOf: Rolled layers of thin polypropylene film coated with a metal film a few nanometres thick, potted in resin inside a plastic case; film is used because it handles high ripple current and heals itself after small breakdowns.

parts.name: DC-link capacitor

parts.description: Cast tray that holds the electronics; coolant flows through channels in its floor.

details.didYouKnow: Mounting the inverter directly on the motor, rather than in a separate box with cables, saves weight and cost and cuts electrical noise because the high-current paths are only centimetres long.
details.howItWorks: The housing is the inverter's backbone and its radiator: the power modules sit on its floor, and coolant from the car's thermal loop flows through channels or pin-fins just beneath them to pull away their heat. It also anchors the control board, capacitor and connectors, and bolts directly onto the motor so the phase busbars can be short.
keyNumbers: Coolant flow typically a few litres per minute through the plate
Must shed up to a few kilowatts of heat at full power
Aluminium conducts heat roughly 4 times better than steel
details.madeOf: High-pressure die-cast aluminium alloy, chosen because it is light, conducts heat well and can be cast with complex internal coolant passages in one piece.

parts.name: Inverter housing

parts.description: Orange-sheathed plug that brings ~350 V DC from the battery pack.

details.didYouKnow: Firefighters and mechanics are trained to treat any orange cable in an electric car as potentially lethal, which is why the colour is used so consistently across brands.
details.howItWorks: Two large pins carry the DC plus and minus from the battery, while a small extra loop of contacts called the high-voltage interlock tells the car whether the plug is fully seated. If the connector is pulled while live, the interlock opens first and the battery contactors switch off before the main pins can arc.
keyNumbers: Carries roughly 350 to 400 V DC
Handles continuous currents of a few hundred amps
Interlock pins are typically a few millimetres shorter than the power pins
details.madeOf: Silver- or tin-plated copper contacts in a glass-filled plastic body, with a braided shield and orange insulation on the cable; orange is the industry's standard warning colour for high voltage.

parts.name: High-voltage connector

parts.description: Copper bar carrying one AC phase from the inverter down to the stator windings.

details.didYouKnow: In a three-phase system no return wire is needed: the current going out along U comes back along V and W, so three bars do the work that six would in separate circuits.
details.howItWorks: Busbar U links the U power module's output to the start of the U winding in the stator. A solid bar is used rather than a cable because it carries hundreds of amps with low resistance and low inductance, and it is often threaded through a current sensor so the control board can measure exactly what is flowing.
keyNumbers: Carries peak currents of very roughly 500 to 1,000 A
Cross-section typically tens of square millimetres
Copper resistivity about 0.017 micro-ohm metres
details.madeOf: Pure copper, often tin-plated at the joints, because copper has the highest conductivity of any affordable metal.

parts.name: Phase busbar U

parts.description: Copper bar carrying one AC phase from the inverter down to the stator windings.

details.didYouKnow: At high frequencies current crowds toward the outside of a conductor (the skin effect), which is one reason designers favour flat bars with lots of surface area.
details.howItWorks: Busbar V feeds the second phase. Its current alternates direction many times per second, with a frequency set by motor speed: the faster the rotor spins, the faster the inverter has to swing the current back and forth along this bar.
keyNumbers: AC frequency up to roughly 1,000 Hz or more at top speed
Joints usually bolted at around 5 to 10 N m
Often only a few centimetres long
details.madeOf: Electrolytic-grade copper strip, stamped and bent to shape, usually sleeved or coated in insulation wherever it passes close to the housing.

parts.name: Phase busbar V

parts.description: Copper bar carrying one AC phase from the inverter down to the stator windings.

details.didYouKnow: Copper for electrical use must be extremely pure, typically over 99.9 percent, because even tiny impurities noticeably increase its resistance.
details.howItWorks: Busbar W carries the third phase down into the motor. The three bars are usually laid out close and parallel so their magnetic fields largely cancel, which keeps stray inductance low and reduces voltage spikes when the transistors switch.
keyNumbers: Heats by only tens of degrees even at full power
Insulation rated well above the roughly 400 V working voltage
Three phases carry equal current, 120 degrees apart
details.madeOf: Copper bar, sometimes laminated together with the other phases and thin insulating sheets into a single sandwich to save space.

parts.name: Phase busbar W

parts.description: Bolted cap closing the far end of the motor; carries the rear bearing.

details.didYouKnow: If the bearing seat were even slightly off-centre, the rotor's magnets would pull harder on one side of the gap, causing noise and vibration.
details.howItWorks: The end cover closes the back of the motor housing and holds the rear bearing exactly on the motor axis, so the rotor stays centred inside the stator with only a small air gap. It often also houses the resolver and has oil passages that drain lubricant from the bearing back to the sump.
keyNumbers: Air gap it helps maintain is typically under 1 mm
Bearing bore machined to within about 0.01 to 0.02 mm
Held by 8 flange bolts in this unit
details.madeOf: Die-cast aluminium, machined precisely at the bearing seat, because it must be light yet hold the bearing within a few hundredths of a millimetre of true.

parts.name: Motor end cover

parts.description: One of eight flange bolts holding the end cover on.

details.didYouKnow: Aluminium expands about twice as much as steel when it heats up, so engineers have to make sure the bolts keep their clamping force as the motor warms and cools.
details.howItWorks: The bolts clamp the end cover to the motor housing, squeezing the seal between them so oil cannot leak out. They are tightened in a criss-cross pattern so the cover seats evenly and the bearing stays aligned.
keyNumbers: Typically about M6 to M8 in size
Tightened to roughly 10 to 25 N m
Usually property class 8.8 or 10.9 steel
details.madeOf: High-strength alloy steel, usually zinc-flake coated to resist corrosion, since it must stay tight through years of heat cycling against aluminium.

parts.name: End cover bolt

parts.description: Position sensor that tells the inverter exactly where the rotor is, so it can time each pulse of current.

details.didYouKnow: Resolvers were developed for aircraft and military equipment because they are so robust, and the same principle now runs in almost every electric car motor.
details.howItWorks: A resolver is a kind of rotary transformer: a coil on the stator side is fed a high-frequency signal, and a shaped steel rotor on the motor shaft changes how strongly that signal couples into two pickup coils set 90 degrees apart. Comparing the two outputs gives the rotor's angle, which the inverter needs to line up the magnetic field with the magnets.
keyNumbers: Excitation signal typically about 10 kHz
Angle accuracy usually a fraction of a degree
Works up to well beyond 18,000 rpm
details.madeOf: Laminated electrical steel and fine enamelled copper wire, with no electronics on the moving part, so it shrugs off heat, oil and vibration.

parts.name: Resolver

parts.description: Ball bearing supporting the rotor shaft at the end-cover side.

details.didYouKnow: Fast-switching inverters can induce small voltages on the motor shaft that spark across a bearing's oil film, leaving a washboard pattern called fluting, so EV bearings often need special protection.
details.howItWorks: This deep-groove ball bearing supports the rotor's far end, while a second bearing near the gearbox supports the other end. It keeps the rotor centred and lets it spin with very little friction, and it is lubricated by the same oil that cools the motor.
keyNumbers: Spins at up to about 18,000 rpm
Ball diameter typically several millimetres
Expected to last the life of the car, often over 300,000 km
details.madeOf: Hardened bearing steel rings and balls; some EV motors use ceramic balls or insulated outer rings to stop stray currents from the inverter pitting the races.

parts.name: Rear rotor bearing

parts.description: Laminated steel cylinder carrying the magnets; it spins up to about 18,000 rpm.

details.didYouKnow: At top speed the outside of the rotor moves faster than a Formula 1 car, so the thin steel bridges holding the magnets in must withstand enormous centrifugal force.
details.howItWorks: The rotor carries the magnets and is pulled round by the rotating magnetic field from the stator. It is built from hundreds of thin steel sheets stacked together so that eddy currents cannot circulate freely, and the slots punched into those sheets both hold the magnets and create the steel paths that produce extra reluctance torque.
keyNumbers: Spins up to about 18,000 rpm
Surface speed at top rpm roughly 500 km/h
Laminations typically about 0.25 to 0.35 mm thick
details.madeOf: Thin silicon-steel laminations stamped, stacked and bonded or welded together, with the magnets glued or held by resin inside their pockets.

parts.name: Rotor core

parts.description: Neodymium magnet buried in the rotor; the V-shaped pairs add reluctance torque to the magnets' pull.

details.didYouKnow: Neodymium magnets lose strength permanently if they get too hot, which is a big reason the motor is cooled so carefully with oil.
details.howItWorks: Each magnet's field locks on to the rotating field produced by the stator, pulling the rotor round. Because the magnets are buried in a V shape rather than glued to the surface, the steel around them also prefers to line up with the stator's field, adding a second source of torque called reluctance torque.
keyNumbers: 12 magnets in this model, in V-shaped pairs
Remanent field typically about 1.2 to 1.4 tesla
Usually rated to work up to roughly 150 to 180 °C
details.madeOf: Sintered neodymium-iron-boron, the strongest commercial permanent magnet, often with a little dysprosium or terbium added so it keeps its strength when hot, plus a nickel or epoxy coating against corrosion.

parts.name: Rotor magnet

parts.description: Hollow steel shaft running from the rotor into the gearbox, where it carries the input gear.

details.didYouKnow: A hollow shaft is almost as stiff in twisting as a solid one of the same outside size, because most of the strength comes from the metal near the outer surface.
details.howItWorks: The shaft runs through the centre of the rotor stack, carries its torque to the gearbox and turns on the two rotor bearings. It is hollow so that oil can be pumped down its middle and flung outward through holes to cool the rotor and magnets from the inside.
keyNumbers: Transmits roughly 300 to 450 N m of motor torque
Typically turns about 4,000 to 5,000 times per km driven
Bore usually around 10 to 20 mm across
details.madeOf: Alloy steel, machined and induction-hardened at the bearing journals and splines; making it hollow saves weight with little loss of stiffness.

parts.name: Rotor shaft

parts.description: Stack of thin electrical-steel laminations with slots that hold the copper windings.

details.didYouKnow: Adding silicon to iron raises its electrical resistance, which shrinks the wasteful eddy currents that would otherwise heat the core.
details.howItWorks: The stator is the stationary ring that surrounds the rotor. When current flows through the copper windings in its slots, the steel teeth channel and concentrate the resulting magnetic field across the narrow air gap to the rotor, and the three phases make that field spin.
keyNumbers: Silicon content typically about 3 percent
Usually around 48 to 72 slots in this class of motor
Stack length roughly 10 to 20 cm
details.madeOf: Hundreds of thin non-oriented silicon-steel laminations, each insulated with a thin coating and stacked into a solid core, to cut the eddy-current losses that a solid block would suffer.

parts.name: Stator core

parts.description: Bent copper hairpins — flat bars welded end to end — forming the three-phase winding.

details.didYouKnow: Hairpin stators are well suited to robots, which is one reason they spread quickly through high-volume EV factories.
details.howItWorks: Instead of winding round wire, U-shaped flat copper bars called hairpins are pushed into the stator slots from one side. Their closed bends form this end of the winding, and the bars pack tightly in the slots, so more copper fits into the same space and the motor makes more torque with less heating.
keyNumbers: Slot fill typically about 70 percent versus about 45 percent for round wire
Bar cross-section roughly a few millimetres by a few millimetres
Enamel insulation only about 0.1 to 0.2 mm thick
details.madeOf: Rectangular enamel-insulated copper bar, bent into shape by machines; the flat profile packs far more tightly than round wire.

parts.name: Hairpin winding end (gearbox side)

parts.description: Welded ends of the hairpin conductors on the other side of the stator.

details.didYouKnow: The exposed end turns are an ideal spot for cooling, so many drive units drip or spray oil straight onto them.
details.howItWorks: On this side the open legs of the hairpins stick out of the stator and are twisted so that each one lines up with a leg from another hairpin. The pairs are then welded together, joining all the separate bars into continuous coils for the three phases.
keyNumbers: A stator typically has a few hundred welds
Each laser weld takes a fraction of a second
Oil sprayed on these end turns removes much of the winding's heat
details.madeOf: The same enamelled copper bar, with the insulation stripped at the tips so they can be laser-welded, then usually coated with resin or varnish to insulate and strengthen the joints.

parts.name: Hairpin winding end (cover side)

parts.description: Cast-aluminium sleeve around the stator; oil sprayed inside it carries the motor's heat away.

details.didYouKnow: Electric motors are often well over 90 percent efficient, but at full power even a few percent loss means several kilowatts of heat that this housing and its oil must carry away.
details.howItWorks: The housing grips the stator firmly so it cannot twist under the reaction torque, and holds the front bearing in line with the end cover. Oil from the pump is sprayed or dripped on the stator and windings inside it, collects in a sump and returns to the heat exchanger.
keyNumbers: Must resist reaction torque of up to about 450 N m
Oil inside typically runs at about 60 to 90 °C
Shrink-fitting heats it to roughly 200 °C during assembly
details.madeOf: High-pressure die-cast aluminium alloy; the stator is often shrink-fitted in by heating the housing so it expands, inserting the stator, and letting it cool to a tight grip.

parts.name: Motor housing

parts.description: Outer half of the gearbox case, sealing in the oil that lubricates the gears and cools the motor.

details.didYouKnow: Without engine noise to mask it, gear whine is one of the loudest sounds in an EV, so engineers shape gearbox casings carefully to keep them quiet.
details.howItWorks: The cover closes the outer side of the gearbox, holding the far bearings of the gear shafts and sealing in the oil. As the gears spin they splash oil up onto its inside walls, from where it trickles back down to lubricate bearings and teeth.
keyNumbers: Gearbox oil fill typically a couple of litres
Oil is low-viscosity, similar to automatic transmission fluid
Sealing face kept flat to within a few hundredths of a millimetre
details.madeOf: Die-cast aluminium with stiffening ribs, which keep it light and help stop it vibrating like a loudspeaker and radiating gear whine.

parts.name: Gearbox cover

parts.description: Inner half of the gearbox case, bolted to the motor housing; it holds the shaft bearings.

details.didYouKnow: Many drive units combine the motor and gearbox housings into shared castings, which cuts parts and joints compared with bolting a separate motor to a separate transmission.
details.howItWorks: The case is the structural heart of the gearbox, bolted to the motor housing and holding the bearings for all three shafts exactly parallel at the right spacing. Accurate bearing positions matter because even small misalignment makes gear teeth wear unevenly and whine.
keyNumbers: Holds 3 parallel shafts: motor, intermediate and differential
Shaft centre distances held to within about 0.02 to 0.05 mm
Resists reaction torque of a few thousand N m at the output
details.madeOf: High-pressure die-cast aluminium, precision-machined at the bearing bores, combining low weight with enough stiffness to keep the gears in mesh under full torque.

parts.name: Gearbox case

parts.description: Small gear on the motor shaft — the first of two reduction stages (about 9:1 overall).

details.didYouKnow: EV gears use helical, slanted teeth so that several teeth are in contact at once, which spreads the load and makes them much quieter than straight-cut gears.
details.howItWorks: The pinion sits on the end of the rotor shaft and turns at full motor speed. It has few teeth, so each turn of the large intermediate gear it drives takes several turns of the pinion, cutting speed and multiplying torque by the same factor.
keyNumbers: Spins up to about 18,000 rpm
Typically has roughly 15 to 25 teeth
Tooth surface hardness around 58 to 62 HRC
details.madeOf: Case-hardened alloy steel: the tooth surfaces are carburised to be very hard and wear-resistant while the core stays tough, then the teeth are precision ground for quiet running.

parts.name: Input pinion

parts.description: Large gear driven by the input pinion; it slows the motor speed about threefold.

details.didYouKnow: Gear teeth are given tiny deliberate shape corrections, called micro-geometry, measured in micrometres, to cancel out bending under load and keep the mesh quiet.
details.howItWorks: This large gear meshes with the input pinion and forms the first reduction stage, turning about a third as fast as the motor. It is fixed to the intermediate shaft, so its torque passes straight to the intermediate pinion beside it.
keyNumbers: First-stage reduction roughly 3:1
Turns at up to about 6,000 rpm
Gear tooth contact efficiency typically about 98 to 99 percent per stage
details.madeOf: Forged, machined and case-hardened alloy steel, with the teeth ground after heat treatment to correct any distortion.

parts.name: Intermediate gear

parts.description: Second-stage pinion sharing the intermediate shaft.

details.didYouKnow: Splitting the reduction into two stages keeps every gear a sensible size; doing 9:1 in one step would need a huge output gear or a tiny, overloaded pinion.
details.howItWorks: The intermediate pinion shares the shaft with the intermediate gear, so it turns at the same speed but, being smaller, pushes harder on the final-drive gear it meshes with. This starts the second reduction stage, where the teeth carry far more force than in the first.
keyNumbers: Second-stage reduction roughly 3:1
Carries roughly 3 times the motor's torque
Typically about 15 to 25 teeth
details.madeOf: Case-hardened alloy steel, usually cut as part of the shaft or pressed on with splines, and made wider than the first-stage gears to cope with the higher torque.

parts.name: Intermediate pinion

parts.description: Shaft carrying the intermediate gear and pinion between their two bearings.

details.didYouKnow: Helical gears push sideways along their shafts as well as round them, so the bearings must resist end-thrust as well as radial load.
details.howItWorks: The intermediate shaft links the two reduction stages, turning the speed-reduced output of the first stage into the input of the second. It spins on two bearings in the gearbox case and cover, and has to stay stiff so its two gears stay correctly meshed.
keyNumbers: Spins at up to about 6,000 rpm
Carries roughly 3 times motor torque
Supported by 2 bearings
details.madeOf: Alloy steel, machined and hardened, with ground bearing journals; tapered roller or ball bearings carry the side forces created by the helical teeth.

parts.name: Intermediate shaft

parts.description: Large gear bolted to the differential; the second reduction stage.

details.didYouKnow: Because an electric motor works across such a wide speed range, this single fixed ratio replaces the whole set of gears a petrol car needs.
details.howItWorks: The final-drive gear is the biggest in the gearbox and is bolted to the differential case. Driven by the intermediate pinion, it completes the overall reduction of about 9:1, so the differential and wheels turn at about one ninth of motor speed with roughly nine times the torque.
keyNumbers: Overall ratio about 9:1
Turns at up to about 2,000 rpm
Output torque can reach very roughly 3,000 to 4,000 N m
details.madeOf: Large case-hardened alloy steel gear, ground for quiet running and bolted or welded to the differential case.

parts.name: Final-drive gear

parts.description: Housing for the differential gears, which let the two rear wheels turn at different speeds in corners.

details.didYouKnow: An open differential sends equal torque to both wheels, so if one wheel is on ice, both get only the little torque the slipping wheel can use; EVs fix this by braking the spinning wheel with traction control.
details.howItWorks: The differential case spins with the final-drive gear and carries a cross pin holding the spider gears. When the car goes straight, everything turns together as one block; in a corner, the spider gears rotate on their pin so the outer wheel can go faster than the inner one while both still get equal torque.
keyNumbers: Carries the full output torque of a few thousand N m
In a tight turn, wheel speeds can differ by about 20 percent or more
Turns at up to about 2,000 rpm
details.madeOf: Usually cast ductile iron or forged steel, both strong and tough enough to carry the full output torque and resist shock loads.

parts.name: Differential case

parts.description: Bevel gear splined to the left axle shaft.

details.didYouKnow: The speeds of the two side gears always average to the speed of the differential case, so if one wheel stops completely, the other spins at twice the case speed.
details.howItWorks: The left side gear meshes with both spider gears and is splined to the left axle. When both wheels turn at the same speed it simply rotates with the case; when the left wheel slows in a left-hand corner, the spider gears roll around it and speed up the right side instead.
keyNumbers: Typically about 14 to 18 teeth
Carries half the output torque, roughly 1,500 to 2,000 N m
Usually backed by a thrust washer a millimetre or two thick
details.madeOf: Forged and case-hardened alloy steel bevel gear, with internal splines broached into its hub to grip the axle.

parts.name: Side gear (left)

parts.description: Bevel gear splined to the right axle shaft.

details.didYouKnow: The idea of the differential is old: one appeared in a steam carriage in France in the 1820s, long before the motor car.
details.howItWorks: The right side gear is the mirror of the left, splined to the right axle. In a right-hand bend the right wheel follows the tighter inner path, so this gear turns more slowly than the case while the left gear turns correspondingly faster.
keyNumbers: Splined hub typically has around 20 to 30 splines
Speed differences in normal corners usually under about 10 percent
Lubricated by splash from the gearbox oil
details.madeOf: Case-hardened alloy steel; bevel teeth are often precision forged nearly to final shape, which saves machining and leaves a strong grain flow in the teeth.

parts.name: Side gear (right)

parts.description: Small bevel gear that rolls between the side gears when the wheels turn at different speeds.

details.didYouKnow: On a straight road the spider gears barely move at all, which is why they can run for hundreds of thousands of kilometres on little more than a splash of oil.
details.howItWorks: The spider gear turns on the cross pin inside the differential case and meshes with both side gears at once. Going straight it does not spin on its pin and just carries the side gears round; in a corner it rotates, letting one side gear speed up as the other slows by the same amount.
keyNumbers: Typically about 9 to 11 teeth
Usually stationary on its pin when driving straight
Bevel teeth meet the side gears at 90 degrees
details.madeOf: Small case-hardened steel bevel gear with a smooth hardened bore that runs directly on the steel cross pin, lubricated by gearbox oil.

parts.name: Spider gear

parts.description: Second spider gear, opposite the first on the cross pin.

details.didYouKnow: If one wheel of a jacked-up car is turned by hand with the other held still, the spider gears spin, and the free wheel turns the opposite way.
details.howItWorks: The second spider gear sits opposite the first on the same cross pin. Having two shares the driving force between two sets of teeth and balances the forces on the side gears, so they are not pushed off-centre.
keyNumbers: 2 spider gears in this differential; heavy-duty ones may have 4
Each shares roughly half the load between the side gears
Spins only as fast as the wheel-speed difference requires
details.madeOf: Identical case-hardened steel to its partner, with a curved spherical back face that sits against a matching thrust washer in the case.

parts.name: Spider gear

parts.description: Hinged latch that locks into a toothed wheel when the car is put in Park.

details.didYouKnow: Because the pawl locks the gearbox rather than the wheels directly, an open differential means a car lifted on one side can still roll; that is why the handbrake is used too.
details.howItWorks: When the driver selects Park, a small actuator pushes this hinged pawl into the teeth of a parking wheel on one of the gearbox shafts, locking the gears and therefore the wheels. Its tooth is shaped so that if the car is still rolling faster than a walking pace it ratchets off rather than engaging and breaking.
keyNumbers: Usually engages only below about 3 to 5 km/h
Locks against a wheel with typically around 10 to 20 notches
Must hold the car on steep gradients of 20 percent or more
details.madeOf: Hardened steel, needed so the narrow tooth can hold the whole car on a slope without bending or wearing.

parts.name: Parking pawl

parts.description: Output shaft to the left wheel; it runs alongside the motor.

details.didYouKnow: A long, slim shaft acts like a torsion spring, twisting slightly under load, which can actually help smooth out sudden jolts of torque.
details.howItWorks: The left axle stub is splined into the left side gear and carries its torque out of the gearbox. Because the gearbox sits off to one side, this shaft runs alongside the motor to reach the far side of the unit, passing through a seal that keeps the oil in.
keyNumbers: Carries up to roughly 1,500 to 2,000 N m
Spins at up to about 2,000 rpm
Typically about 25 to 35 mm diameter
details.madeOf: Induction-hardened medium-carbon alloy steel, which gives a hard, fatigue-resistant surface on the splines while the core stays tough enough to twist slightly without breaking.

parts.name: Left axle stub

parts.description: Short output shaft to the right wheel.

details.didYouKnow: Unequal-length shafts can make a car tug sideways under hard acceleration, called torque steer, but with rear-wheel drive this has very little effect on steering.
details.howItWorks: The right stub is much shorter because the differential sits on the right side of the unit. It takes torque from the right side gear and passes it through a lip seal to the right output flange.
keyNumbers: Often only around 10 to 20 cm long
Turns about 470 times per kilometre with a typical tyre
Seal lip runs on a surface polished to a fine finish
details.madeOf: Forged and machined alloy steel, splined at both ends and hardened where seals and bearings run.

parts.name: Right axle stub

parts.description: Joint where the left half-shaft to the wheel plugs in.

details.didYouKnow: A plain universal joint makes the output shaft speed up and slow down twice per turn when it is bent; a constant-velocity joint cancels this so the wheel turns smoothly.
details.howItWorks: This flange is where the left half-shaft connects. The half-shaft has constant-velocity joints at each end, so the wheel can move up and down on the suspension and the drive keeps turning smoothly without its speed pulsing.
keyNumbers: Allows joint angles of roughly 20 degrees or more
Passes up to roughly 2,000 N m to the wheel
CV joints often have 6 steel balls
details.madeOf: Forged steel, splined to the axle stub and machined where the joint or boot attaches.

parts.name: Left output flange

parts.description: Joint where the right half-shaft to the wheel plugs in.

details.didYouKnow: A torn CV boot is one of the most common drivetrain faults; once dirt gets into the grease, the joint wears out quickly.
details.howItWorks: The right output flange connects the right half-shaft, which runs out to the right rear hub. Its inner joint can usually slide in and out a little to allow for the change in shaft length as the suspension moves.
keyNumbers: Plunge travel typically a few centimetres
Spins at up to about 2,000 rpm
Boot holds roughly 100 g or more of grease
details.madeOf: Forged and hardened steel; the joint itself is packed with grease and protected by a flexible rubber or plastic boot.

parts.name: Right output flange

parts.description: Cast bracket bolting the drive unit to the car's rear subframe.

details.didYouKnow: When you accelerate hard, the whole drive unit tries to rotate the opposite way to the wheels, so its mounts work hardest during launches and regenerative braking.
details.howItWorks: The bracket bolts the drive unit to the car's rear subframe, carrying its weight and resisting its tendency to twist when it delivers torque to the wheels. It works together with rubber bushings so the unit is held firmly but not rigidly.
keyNumbers: Supports a drive unit weighing roughly 80 to 100 kg
Resists reaction torque of a few thousand N m
Usually held by bolts of about M10 to M12
details.madeOf: Cast aluminium, shaped with ribs for stiffness at low weight; casting allows complex shapes that put metal only where loads flow.

parts.name: Mounting bracket

parts.description: Rubber bushing that stops motor whine and vibration reaching the cabin.

details.didYouKnow: EV cabins are so quiet that motor whine at a few kilohertz becomes noticeable, so drive-unit mounts are tuned more carefully than engine mounts once were.
details.howItWorks: The bushing is a rubber cushion between the bracket and the subframe. It is stiff enough to stop the unit moving much under torque, but soft enough to absorb the high-pitched whine and vibration from the motor and gears before they reach the body.
keyNumbers: Rubber hardness typically about 50 to 70 Shore A
Allows movement of only a few millimetres
Targets noise from a few hundred to a few thousand hertz
details.madeOf: Natural or synthetic rubber bonded to steel or aluminium sleeves; rubber is chosen because it absorbs vibration energy rather than passing it on.

parts.name: Rubber mount bushing

parts.description: Electric pump that circulates gearbox oil over the gears and through the motor to cool it.

details.didYouKnow: Some drive units can deliberately run the motor inefficiently to make extra heat, which the oil and coolant loop then use to warm the battery in cold weather.
details.howItWorks: The pump draws oil from the gearbox sump, pushes it through the filter and heat exchanger, and delivers it to jets and passages that spray the stator windings, flow down the hollow rotor shaft, and lubricate the bearings and gears. Being electric, it can run at any speed the control system chooses, even when the car is stopped.
keyNumbers: Typically flows a few litres per minute
Pressure usually only about 1 to 3 bar
Draws power on the order of tens of watts
details.madeOf: A small brushless electric motor driving a gerotor or gear pump, in a plastic or aluminium body sealed against the oil.

parts.name: Oil pump

parts.description: Screw-in filter that catches wear particles from the gears.

details.didYouKnow: Most of the metal particles in a new gearbox come from the first few hundred kilometres, as the gear teeth bed in against each other.
details.howItWorks: All the oil from the pump passes through the filter, which traps tiny metal particles worn from gear teeth and bearings, as well as any debris left from manufacturing. Clean oil keeps the bearings and gear surfaces from being scratched and stops particles reaching the motor windings.
keyNumbers: Filters particles down to roughly 20 to 40 micrometres
Service intervals can be very long, often over 100,000 km
Contains a bypass valve that opens if the element clogs
details.madeOf: A pleated paper or synthetic-fibre element inside a painted steel canister, often with a magnet nearby to grab steel particles.

parts.name: Oil filter

parts.description: Stack of thin plates where hot motor oil gives its heat to the car's coolant loop.

details.didYouKnow: Oil cools the motor well because it does not conduct electricity and can touch the windings directly, but water-glycol carries heat away much better, so EVs use both.
details.howItWorks: Hot oil from the motor and gears flows through alternate layers of this plate stack, while water-glycol coolant from the car flows through the layers in between. Heat passes through the thin metal walls from oil to coolant, and the coolant carries it to the radiator or to wherever the car needs heat.
keyNumbers: Plates typically well under 1 mm thick
Can move a few kilowatts of heat
Usually has tens of plates
details.madeOf: Thin aluminium plates brazed together in a furnace into one leak-tight block, because aluminium is light and conducts heat very well.

parts.name: Oil-to-coolant heat exchanger

parts.description: Brings coolant from the radiator loop into the heat exchanger and inverter.

details.didYouKnow: Many EVs route the same coolant through the battery, cabin heater and drive unit, using valves to share heat between them.
details.howItWorks: This hose brings cooled water-glycol from the car's thermal system into the drive unit. It typically passes first under the inverter's power modules, which are most sensitive to heat, and then on to the oil heat exchanger.
keyNumbers: Coolant is typically about 50 percent water, 50 percent glycol
Flow usually around 10 to 20 litres per minute
Inlet temperature normally below about 65 °C
details.madeOf: Reinforced EPDM rubber, which resists heat, glycol and ageing while staying flexible enough to absorb vibration between the drive unit and car body.

parts.name: Coolant inlet hose

parts.description: Returns warmed coolant to the car's thermal system.

details.didYouKnow: Glycol in the coolant lowers its freezing point to well below minus 30 °C and also raises its boiling point.
details.howItWorks: The outlet hose carries coolant away after it has collected heat from the inverter and the motor oil. That warm coolant either goes to the radiator to dump heat, or, in cold weather, to the battery or cabin, so the drive unit's waste heat is not entirely wasted.
keyNumbers: Coolant leaves typically a few to about 10 °C warmer than it entered
Hose bore usually around 16 to 25 mm
Rated for system pressures up to about 2 bar
details.madeOf: Reinforced EPDM rubber hose with quick-connect fittings, which allow fast assembly on the factory line.

parts.name: Coolant outlet hose

summary: The motor, inverter and gearbox that replace the engine in an electric car, modelled on the rear drive unit in cars like the Tesla Model 3: a permanent-magnet motor spinning up to 18,000 rpm, a silicon-carbide inverter, and a 9:1 two-stage gearbox with differential.
